newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin sees Yeltsin leaving hospital next week.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin sees Yeltsin leaving hospital next week.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin is recovering steadily from pneumonia and is set to leave hospital soon, the Kremlin said on Friday, but warned that he should not be hurried because of the risk of a relapse.

"It will be in the next few days, but not at the weekend," presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing nine days after Yeltsin was taken to hospital with what doctors said were the first signs of the illness in his lungs.
Yastrzhembsky declined to be more specific. Yeltsin's hospital stay has already been extended once and the Kremlin is now wary of naming a day for his release.
"The president is certainly interested in recovering as quickly as possible," he said.
"But I think it is natural to...show some patience, to give him the chance of recovering completely. A relapse is very dangerous and God forbid that there should be such a relapse.
"His condition is steadily improving. He worked on documents for around three hours (today)...We have no reason to think that the doctors' optimism is unfounded."
Yeltsin's return to hospital on January 8, just two weeks after he resumed work in the Kremlin after heart surgery, has renewed pressure on him to resign because of ill health.

But Yastrzhembsky said the president, who was out of the Kremlin for six months last year with heart problems, did not take seriously opposition calls for him to resign or one communist deputy's bid to try to force him out through a parliamentary motion.

"From the beginning he thought it was more an attempt to play on his nerves than seriously aimed at a political result," Yastrzhembsky said of the motion, which parliamentary experts say would lack legal weight even if adopted.
Russia's post-communist constitution makes it almost impossible for Yeltsin, who turns 66 on February 1, to be removed under the current balance of forces in parliament.

It also concentrates huge powers in his hands and many Western economists have joined Yeltsin's rivals in charging that Russia's reform programme has slowed during his prolonged absences from the Kremlin.

On Friday Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin reassured them reforms would continue. "The West should not worry. Reforms are not stopping, it's just that we don't have much money. But the desire (to reform) is great," he told reporters.
"There have been reforms and there will be reforms. There will be no U-turns in Russia," he said.
Yasztrzembsky said that if Yeltsin's recovery continued at the same rate, he would resume his weekly meetings with Chernomyrdin next week. They normally take place on Tuesdays.

The doctors had allowed the president to move around more and he had even taken part in a family celebration of his daughter Tatyana's birthday in the Central Clinical Hospital near Moscow where he is being treated.
Yeltsin had multiple heart bypass surgery on November 8, but doctors say his pneumonia is not connected with the operation.
Yastrzembsky said he thought he would be well enough to attend a summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), which loosely groups 12 of the 15 ex-Soviet republics.

CIS prime ministers met in Moscow on Friday to pave the way for the end-of-January summit, five years after the creation of the Commonwealth. But several countries disagreed with guidelines for integration, casting doubt over its future direction.

As Yeltsin recovered in hospital, tensions increased around preparations for post-war elections next month in the breakaway Chechnya region, where tens of thousands died in a conflict between rebels and Russian troops, who have now withdrawn.

Reflecting growing concern about the possiblity of a victory by a radical separatist, Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said on Friday that Russia should send troops back to Chechnya if Russians still living in the breakaway region come under attack.
